rooms.about: This year you will read stories, poems, plays and nonfiction more closely, and write arguments, explanations and narratives with clear structure. You will also grow your vocabulary, grammar and speaking skills.

learn: Close reading means reading a text slowly, more than once, and paying attention to details. Good readers ask questions as they read: Who is speaking? What just changed? Why did the author include this?

Text evidence is a quote or detail from the text that supports an idea. When you make a claim about a text, you should point to the exact words that prove it. A strong answer says the claim, gives the evidence, and explains how the evidence supports the claim.

An inference is a smart guess based on clues in the text plus what you already know. If a character slams a door and refuses to speak, you can infer that the character is angry, even if the text never says the word angry.
When you quote, copy the words exactly and put them in quotation marks. When you paraphrase, restate the idea in your own words. Either way, you are showing where your idea came from.
units.try: Pick a short story or chapter you like. Write one sentence about how the main character feels at the end. Then find one quote that proves it and write two sentences explaining how that quote shows the feeling.
check: A conclusion based on text clues and what you know
A direct quote copied from a book
What should follow a quote in a strong answer?
An explanation of how it supports your claim
Nothing; the quote speaks for itself

learn: The theme is the message or lesson about life that a story shows. It is usually not stated directly. A topic is one word, like friendship; a theme is a full idea, like true friends tell you hard truths.
To find a theme, look at how the main character changes, what problem they face, and what they learn. Ask: what does the author want readers to understand about people or life?
A summary is a short retelling of the most important ideas in your own words. It includes the main events or points in order and leaves out small details and your personal opinions.
An objective summary stays neutral. Instead of writing that the story was boring, you report what happened: who, what, where, and how the conflict was resolved.
units.try: Think of a fable or folktale you know, such as the tortoise and the hare. Write a three-sentence objective summary. Then write the theme as a complete sentence, not just one word.
check: Which is a theme rather than a topic?
Hard work can beat natural talent
What should an objective summary leave out?

units.t: Characters, Plot and Point of View
learn: Plot is the sequence of events in a story. It usually has exposition (setting and characters), rising action, a climax (the turning point), falling action, and a resolution.
Characters respond to conflict, and their choices move the plot forward. A dynamic character changes during the story; a static character stays mostly the same.

Point of view is who tells the story. First person uses I and we, and the narrator is a character. Third person uses he, she and they; a third-person omniscient narrator knows every character’s thoughts, while third-person limited follows just one.
The point of view shapes what readers know. A first-person narrator may not understand everything, which can create surprise or humor.
units.try: Rewrite a short scene from a story you know in a different point of view. For example, retell a moment from the first person of a side character. Notice what the new narrator would know and not know.
check: What is the climax of a story?
The turning point of the conflict
Which pronoun signals first-person point of view?

learn: Figurative language means words used in a non-literal way to create a picture or feeling. A simile compares two things using like or as: her voice was like warm honey. A metaphor compares directly: the classroom was a zoo.
Personification gives human qualities to things that are not human: the wind whispered. Hyperbole is extreme exaggeration: I have told you a million times.
Connotation is the feeling a word carries, while denotation is its dictionary meaning. Thrifty and stingy both mean careful with money, but thrifty sounds positive and stingy sounds negative.
Authors choose words to set a tone, which is the author’s attitude, such as playful, serious or angry. Changing one word can change the whole mood of a sentence.
units.try: Write four sentences about the weather today: one simile, one metaphor, one personification and one hyperbole. Underline (or say aloud) which is which.
check: The snow was as soft as a pillow
Which word has a more negative connotation than curious?

units.t: Reading Nonfiction: Main Idea and Structure
learn: Informational texts teach facts about real topics. The central idea is the most important point the author makes. Supporting details, such as facts, examples and statistics, explain or prove it.
Authors organize nonfiction with text structures. Common ones are chronological (time order), cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution, and description.
Text features help you find information: headings, captions, bold words, diagrams, charts and a glossary. Read them before and after the main text.
Authors have a purpose: to inform, to persuade or to entertain. Notice whether the writer presents both sides or only one, and what evidence they use.
units.try: Find a short news article or encyclopedia entry about an animal. Write its central idea in one sentence, list three supporting details, and name the text structure it mostly uses.
check: Which text structure explains why something happened and what resulted?
Explain or prove the central idea

learn: An argument tries to convince readers to accept a claim. A claim is a clear statement of your position, such as: our school should have a longer recess.
Support your claim with reasons and evidence. Reasons explain why; evidence proves it with facts, data, examples or expert quotes. Credible sources are accurate and trustworthy.
Strong arguments address a counterclaim, which is an opposing view. You state it fairly and then explain why your claim is still stronger.

Organize your essay with an introduction that states the claim, body paragraphs for each reason, and a conclusion that restates the claim and leaves the reader with something to think about. Use transitions like first, in addition, however and therefore.
units.try: Choose a question, such as whether students should have homework on weekends. Write a claim, two reasons with one piece of evidence each, and one counterclaim with your response.
check: An opposing view to your claim
Which is the best evidence for an argument?
A statistic from a trustworthy source
A guess about what people think

learn: Informative writing explains a topic or teaches how something works. It is based on facts, not opinions.
Start with an introduction that names the topic and previews the main points. Then write body paragraphs, each with a topic sentence and details such as definitions, facts, examples and quotes.
Use precise vocabulary related to the topic and define words your reader may not know. Headings, lists and diagrams can make complex information easier to follow.
Keep a formal style: avoid slang and phrases like I think. End with a conclusion that sums up the main points and explains why the topic matters.
units.try: Write a five-sentence paragraph explaining how to care for a houseplant or pet. Begin with a topic sentence, give three specific facts or steps, and end with a concluding sentence.
check: Informative writing is mainly based on what?
Which belongs in a formal informative essay?

learn: A narrative tells a story, real or imagined. It needs a narrator, characters, a setting, a conflict, and a series of events that build to a resolution.
Narrative techniques bring a story to life. Dialogue shows characters talking. Description uses sensory details: sight, sound, smell, taste and touch. Pacing controls how fast or slow time moves.
Show, don’t tell: instead of writing she was nervous, write her hands shook as she held the paper. Readers enjoy figuring out feelings from actions.
Use transition words to signal shifts in time or setting, such as later that night or meanwhile. End with a conclusion that reflects on what happened.
units.try: Write a half-page story about a time something did not go as planned. Include at least two lines of dialogue and one sentence that shows a feeling through action instead of naming it.
check: What does show, don’t tell mean?
Reveal feelings through actions and details
The bread smelled warm and sweet

learn: Pronouns replace nouns. Subject pronouns (I, he, she, we, they) do the action; object pronouns (me, him, her, us, them) receive it. Correct: She and I went. Correct: The coach called her and me.
A pronoun must clearly agree with the noun it replaces in number. Each student brought his or her book, or All students brought their books. Avoid vague pronouns when it is unclear who they means.
Commas, parentheses and dashes can set off extra information: My aunt, a nurse, works nights. Use a comma before and, but, or so when joining two complete sentences.
Vary your sentences. Mix simple sentences (one clause) with compound sentences (two clauses joined by and, but, or) and complex sentences (with because, when, although).
units.try: Fix these: Me and him went to the park. Then combine these two sentences into one complex sentence: It rained. We stayed inside. (Answers: He and I went to the park. Because it rained, we stayed inside.)
check: She and I finished the project
Her and me finished the project
Me and her finished the project
Which word could make a complex sentence?

learn: Poems use lines and stanzas instead of paragraphs. Sound devices include rhyme, rhythm, repetition and alliteration, which is the repeating of first sounds, like silly snakes slither.

Drama is written to be performed. A script has a cast of characters, dialogue, and stage directions in parentheses or italics that tell actors how to move or speak. Plays are divided into acts and scenes.
In a discussion, come prepared, listen fully, ask questions that build on others’ ideas, and respond respectfully even when you disagree.
When presenting, speak clearly at a steady pace, make eye contact, and organize your talk with an opening, main points and a closing. Visuals should support, not replace, your words.
units.try: Write a short poem of two four-line stanzas about a place you love, using at least one example of alliteration. Then read it aloud to someone, practicing slow, clear speech.
check: Repeating the first sounds of nearby words
A rhyme at the end of lines
What do stage directions tell actors?

rooms.about: This year you will master ratios, rates and percents, divide fractions, work with negative numbers, and begin algebra with expressions and equations. You will also study area, volume and basic statistics.

learn: A ratio compares two quantities. If a class has 12 girls and 10 boys, the ratio of girls to boys is 12 to 10, which can be written 12:10 or 12/10.
Equivalent ratios name the same comparison. Multiply or divide both parts by the same number: 12:10 = 6:5 = 24:20. A ratio table lists equivalent ratios in rows or columns.
Ratios can compare part to part (girls to boys, 12:10) or part to whole (girls to all students, 12:22). Read carefully to know which one a question asks for.
You can solve ratio problems with tables, tape diagrams or double number lines. Each shows how two amounts grow together at the same rate.
units.try: A recipe uses 2 cups of flour for every 3 cups of milk. How much milk for 8 cups of flour? Step 1: 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so the recipe is scaled by 4. Step 2: 3 × 4 = 12. Answer: 12 cups of milk. Now try: how much flour for 15 cups of milk?
check: A bag has 5 red and 7 blue marbles. What is the ratio of red to all marbles?

learn: A rate compares quantities with different units, like 150 miles in 3 hours. A unit rate tells the amount for one unit: 150 ÷ 3 = 50 miles per hour.
Unit rates help compare prices. If 4 pens cost $6, the unit price is $6 ÷ 4 = $1.50 per pen. The lower unit price is the better buy.
A percent is a rate per 100. 35% means 35 out of 100, or 0.35, or 35/100. To find a percent of a number, multiply: 20% of 60 = 0.20 × 60 = 12.
To find the whole when you know a part, divide: if 30 is 25% of a number, the number is 30 ÷ 0.25 = 120.
units.try: A jacket costs $80 and is 25% off. Step 1: 25% of 80 = 0.25 × 80 = $20. Step 2: 80 − 20 = $60. The sale price is $60. Now try: what is 15% of $40?
check: A car travels 240 miles in 4 hours. What is the unit rate?

learn: Dividing by a fraction asks how many of that fraction fit into a number. For example, 3 ÷ ½ asks how many halves are in 3. The answer is 6.
To divide fractions, multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor. The reciprocal flips the numerator and denominator: the reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2. Many people remember this as keep, change, flip.
Example: 3/4 ÷ 1/8 = 3/4 × 8/1 = 24/4 = 6. So six eighths fit in three fourths.
For mixed numbers, first change them to improper fractions: 2½ = 5/2. Then divide as usual and simplify the answer.
units.try: Solve 2/3 ÷ 4/9. Step 1: keep 2/3. Step 2: change ÷ to ×. Step 3: flip 4/9 to 9/4. Step 4: 2/3 × 9/4 = 18/12 = 3/2 = 1½. Now try 5/6 ÷ 1/3.

learn: To add or subtract decimals, line up the decimal points. To multiply, multiply as whole numbers and then count the total decimal places in both factors: 1.2 × 0.3 = 0.36.
To divide by a decimal, move the decimal point in the divisor to make it whole, and move it the same number of places in the dividend: 4.8 ÷ 0.6 becomes 48 ÷ 6 = 8.
The greatest common factor (GCF) is the largest number that divides two numbers evenly. The GCF of 12 and 18 is 6.
The least common multiple (LCM) is the smallest number both numbers divide into. The LCM of 4 and 6 is 12. LCM helps find common denominators; GCF helps simplify fractions.
units.try: Find the GCF and LCM of 8 and 12. Factors of 8: 1, 2, 4, 8. Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. GCF = 4. Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. Multiples of 12: 12, 24. LCM = 24. Now try 6 and 10.
check: What is the GCF of 15 and 25?

units.t: Negative Numbers and the Coordinate Plane
learn: Integers include positive whole numbers, negative whole numbers and zero. Negative numbers describe values below zero, such as −10°F or a debt of $5.
On a number line, numbers increase to the right. So −2 is greater than −7. Opposites are the same distance from zero on opposite sides: 4 and −4.
Absolute value is a number’s distance from zero, so it is never negative: |−9| = 9 and |9| = 9.
The coordinate plane has an x-axis and a y-axis that cross at the origin (0, 0). A point (3, −2) means move 3 right and 2 down. The axes divide the plane into four quadrants.
units.try: Plot these on graph paper: A(2, 3), B(−2, 3), C(−2, −3), D(2, −3). Connect them. You made a rectangle 4 units wide and 6 units tall. What is its perimeter? (20 units)

learn: A variable is a letter that stands for a number. An expression combines numbers, variables and operations, like 3x + 5. It has no equal sign.
An exponent shows repeated multiplication: 2⁴ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. The base is 2 and the exponent is 4.
Order of operations: parentheses first, then exponents, then multiplication and division from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right. 3 + 4 × 2 = 11, not 14.
To evaluate an expression, substitute a value for the variable. If x = 4, then 3x + 5 = 3 × 4 + 5 = 17.
units.try: Evaluate 2(n + 3)² when n = 1. Step 1: parentheses, 1 + 3 = 4. Step 2: exponent, 4² = 16. Step 3: multiply, 2 × 16 = 32. Now try 5 + 2³ × 3.

learn: Equivalent expressions have the same value for any value of the variable. For example, 2(x + 3) and 2x + 6 are equivalent.
The distributive property says a(b + c) = ab + ac. You can use it to expand, like 4(y + 2) = 4y + 8, or to factor, like 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3).
Like terms have the same variable part. You can combine 3x + 5x = 8x, but you cannot combine 3x + 5 into one term.
Writing expressions from words: five more than a number is n + 5; twice a number is 2n; a number divided by 3 is n/3.
units.try: Simplify 3(x + 4) + 2x. Step 1: distribute, 3x + 12 + 2x. Step 2: combine like terms, 5x + 12. Check with x = 1: 3(5) + 2 = 17 and 5 + 12 = 17. Now simplify 2(a + 5) + 3a.

learn: An equation says two expressions are equal, like x + 7 = 12. A solution is a value that makes it true. Here x = 5.
To solve, use inverse operations to get the variable alone. Undo addition with subtraction and multiplication with division. Do the same thing to both sides to keep the balance.
Example: 4x = 28. Divide both sides by 4: x = 7. Example: y − 3 = 10. Add 3 to both sides: y = 13.
An inequality uses <, >, ≤ or ≥. x > 3 has infinitely many solutions, shown on a number line with an open circle at 3 and an arrow to the right. ≤ and ≥ use a closed circle.
units.try: Solve x/5 = 6. Step 1: the variable is divided by 5, so multiply both sides by 5. Step 2: x = 30. Check: 30 ÷ 5 = 6. Now solve 9 + m = 21.

learn: Area is the space inside a flat shape, in square units. Rectangle: A = l × w. Triangle: A = ½ × b × h. Parallelogram: A = b × h.
To find the area of a complex shape, split it into rectangles and triangles, find each area, then add.
Surface area is the total area of all faces of a 3D shape. A net is a flat pattern that folds into the shape; add the areas of each face in the net.
Volume is the space inside a solid, in cubic units. For a rectangular prism, V = l × w × h. A box 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm holds 24 cubic centimeters. This also works with fractional edge lengths.
units.try: Find the area of a triangle with base 10 m and height 6 m. Step 1: ½ × 10 = 5. Step 2: 5 × 6 = 30. Area = 30 square meters. Now find the volume of a box 5 in by 2 in by 3 in.
check: What is the area of a 7 by 3 rectangle?
What is the volume of a 2 × 2 × 5 prism?

learn: A statistical question expects variety in the answers. How tall are the students in my class? is statistical. How tall am I? is not.
Measures of center describe a typical value. The mean is the sum divided by the count. The median is the middle value when data are in order.
Measures of spread show how varied data are. The range is maximum minus minimum. The interquartile range (IQR) is the third quartile minus the first quartile.
Data displays include dot plots, histograms and box plots. A box plot shows the minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile and maximum.
units.try: Data: 4, 8, 6, 2, 10. Mean: 4 + 8 + 6 + 2 + 10 = 30, and 30 ÷ 5 = 6. Median: order them 2, 4, 6, 8, 10; middle is 6. Range: 10 − 2 = 8. Now try 3, 9, 5, 7.

rooms.about: This year you will explore Earth’s place in space, the rock cycle, plate tectonics, water, weather and climate. You will also study natural resources, natural hazards and how people affect the planet.

learn: The solar system is the Sun and everything that orbits it: eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets like Pluto, asteroids and comets. The four inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are rocky; the four outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are giant planets made mostly of gas or ice.

Gravity is a force of attraction between all objects with mass. The more mass an object has, the stronger its pull. The Sun holds about 99.8% of the solar system’s mass, so its gravity keeps the planets in orbit.
An orbit is the curved path of one object around another. Earth orbits the Sun once every 365.25 days, at an average distance of about 150 million kilometers.
Scientists use models because distances in space are huge. If the Sun were a basketball, Earth would be a peppercorn about 26 meters away.
units.try: Make a scale model of distances on a long strip of paper or a hallway. Mark the Sun at one end, then place the planets in order. Notice how crowded the inner planets are and how far apart the outer ones are.
check: What keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
Which planet is a rocky inner planet?

units.t: Earth, Moon and Sun: Seasons, Phases and Eclipses
learn: Earth rotates on its axis once about every 24 hours, causing day and night. Earth’s axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees.
Seasons are caused by this tilt, not by distance from the Sun. When your hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, sunlight hits more directly and days are longer, so it is summer.
The Moon orbits Earth about every 27 days and reflects sunlight. As it moves, we see different amounts of its lit side; these are phases, from new moon to full moon and back in about 29.5 days.

A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, blocking sunlight. A lunar eclipse happens when Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, and Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon. Never look directly at the Sun, even during an eclipse.
units.try: In a dark room, use a lamp as the Sun and a ball on a pencil as the Moon. Hold the ball at arm’s length and turn slowly in a circle. Watch the lit part of the ball change through the phases.
check: Earth’s changing distance from the Sun
During a solar eclipse, what is between the Sun and Earth?

learn: A star is a huge ball of hot gas that makes energy by nuclear fusion, joining hydrogen into helium. The Sun is a medium-sized, middle-aged star about 4.6 billion years old.
Stars differ in size, temperature and brightness. Color shows temperature: blue stars are hottest, and red stars are coolest.
A galaxy is a giant system of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. We live in the Milky Way, a spiral galaxy with hundreds of billions of stars.
Space distances are measured in light-years, the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometers. The nearest star beyond the Sun is about 4.2 light-years away.
units.try: On a clear night, go outside with an adult and look for stars of different colors. Let your eyes adjust for 10 minutes. Can you spot a reddish star and a bluish-white one?
check: The distance light travels in one year
What galaxy do we live in?

units.t: Minerals, Rocks and the Rock Cycle
learn: A mineral is a naturally formed, inorganic solid with a definite chemical makeup and crystal structure. Quartz and feldspar are common minerals. Geologists identify minerals by color, streak, luster and hardness.

Rocks are made of minerals. Igneous rock forms when melted rock (magma or lava) cools. Sedimentary rock forms when layers of sediment are pressed and cemented together. Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change an existing rock.
The rock cycle shows how rocks change from one type to another over long periods. Weathering breaks rock into sediment, erosion moves it, and deposition drops it in new places.
Granite and basalt are igneous; sandstone and limestone are sedimentary; marble and slate are metamorphic. Fossils are usually found in sedimentary rock.
units.try: Collect three pebbles from outside. Wash them and look with a magnifying glass. Do you see layers (maybe sedimentary), crystals (maybe igneous) or bands and stripes (maybe metamorphic)?
check: Which rock forms from cooled magma or lava?
Where are fossils most often found?

learn: Earth has layers: a thin crust, a thick hot mantle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core. The crust and upper mantle form the lithosphere, which is broken into large pieces called tectonic plates.

Plates move a few centimeters per year, about as fast as fingernails grow. At divergent boundaries plates move apart; at convergent boundaries they push together; at transform boundaries they slide past each other.

Evidence for moving plates includes matching fossils and rocks on continents now far apart, the fit of continents like South America and Africa, and the pattern of earthquakes and volcanoes along plate edges.

Earthquakes happen when rocks along a fault suddenly slip. Volcanoes form where magma reaches the surface, often at convergent boundaries or hot spots like Hawaii. Mountains like the Himalayas form where plates collide.
units.try: Take two graham crackers or pieces of cardboard on a plate of frosting or soft clay. Push them together, pull them apart and slide them past each other. Watch what each motion does to the edges.
check: What happens at a divergent boundary?
Which is evidence for plate movement?

learn: Weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces. Mechanical weathering is physical, such as ice wedging in cracks. Chemical weathering changes the minerals, such as acid rain dissolving limestone.
Erosion moves sediment from one place to another by water, wind, ice or gravity. Rivers carve valleys, glaciers scrape land, and waves shape coastlines.
Rock layers record history. The law of superposition says that in undisturbed layers, the oldest are at the bottom and the youngest at the top.
Earth is about 4.6 billion years old. Scientists divide this time into the geologic time scale, using fossils and radioactive dating to place events in order.
units.try: Fill a clear jar with water and add a handful each of sand, soil and small pebbles. Shake it and let it settle overnight. Which layer settles first? This is how sediment layers form.
check: In undisturbed rock layers, where are the oldest layers?
Which is an example of erosion?

units.t: The Water Cycle and Earth’s Water
learn: About 71% of Earth’s surface is covered with water, but about 97% of all water is salty ocean water. Only about 3% is fresh, and most of that is frozen in ice sheets and glaciers.
The water cycle moves water around Earth, powered by the Sun and gravity. Water evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation, and collects in oceans, lakes, groundwater and ice.
Transpiration is water released by plants through their leaves. Runoff is water that flows over land into streams and rivers. Infiltration is water soaking into the ground to become groundwater.
Ocean currents move water and heat around the world. Warm currents like the Gulf Stream carry heat from the tropics toward the poles, affecting climates on land.
units.try: Put a little warm water in a bowl, cover it with plastic wrap, and put ice cubes on top. After 15 minutes, look for droplets under the wrap. You made evaporation and condensation happen.

learn: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a certain time and place: temperature, precipitation, wind, humidity and air pressure. Climate is the average weather of a region over 30 years or more.
Air masses are large bodies of air with similar temperature and moisture. Where two air masses meet is a front. Cold fronts often bring short, strong storms; warm fronts bring longer, gentler rain.
Unequal heating of Earth by the Sun causes wind and global circulation. Latitude, nearness to oceans, elevation and ocean currents all shape a region’s climate.
Meteorologists use instruments: a thermometer measures temperature, a barometer measures air pressure, an anemometer measures wind speed, and a rain gauge measures rainfall.
units.try: Keep a weather journal for one week. Each day at the same time, record the temperature, the clouds, the wind and any rain. At the end, look for patterns before a change in weather.

learn: Natural resources are materials from Earth that people use. Renewable resources, such as sunlight, wind and trees, can be replaced in a human lifetime. Nonrenewable resources, such as coal, oil and natural gas, take millions of years to form.

Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere. Scientists have measured that Earth’s average temperature has risen about 1.1°C since the late 1800s.
People also affect Earth through land use, pollution of air and water, and loss of habitats. Growing populations use more resources.
Solutions include using energy efficiently, switching to renewable energy, recycling, protecting habitats and reducing waste. Engineers design and test solutions and compare their costs and benefits.
units.try: Do a home energy hunt. List every device plugged in at home. Mark which ones could be switched off when not in use. Share your list with your family.
check: What gas from burning fossil fuels traps heat?

learn: Natural hazards are natural events that can harm people: earthquakes, volcanoes, floods, hurricanes, tornadoes, wildfires and droughts.

Scientists study where and when hazards happen to forecast them. Hurricanes can be tracked by satellite for days. Tornado warnings may give minutes. Earthquakes cannot yet be predicted precisely, but maps show where they are likely.
Engineering can reduce harm. Examples are buildings designed to sway in earthquakes, levees against floods and warning sirens.
Every family should have a plan: an emergency kit with water, food, a flashlight and first-aid supplies, a meeting place, and knowledge of what to do. In an earthquake: drop, cover and hold on.
units.try: With your family, make an emergency plan. List what goes in a kit, pick a meeting place outside your home, and practice drop, cover and hold on under a sturdy table.
check: What should you do during an earthquake?
Stand in a doorway on a balcony
Which hazard can be tracked by satellite for days?

rooms.about: This year you will learn the tools of geography and travel back in time to the first humans and the great ancient civilizations of Mesopotamia, Egypt, India, China, Greece, Rome and the Americas.

learn: Geography is the study of Earth’s places, people and environments. Geographers use five themes: location, place, region, movement, and human-environment interaction.

Absolute location uses latitude and longitude. Lines of latitude run east-west and measure distance north or south of the equator. Lines of longitude run north-south and measure distance east or west of the prime meridian.
Maps have a title, a compass rose, a scale and a legend (key). Every flat map distorts Earth somewhat, because a globe’s curved surface cannot be flattened perfectly.
Earth has seven continents (Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, South America) and five oceans (Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, Arctic).
units.try: Find your town on a map or globe. Estimate its latitude and longitude. Then name the continent and nearest ocean, and describe one way people in your area have changed the environment.
check: What do lines of latitude measure?
Distance north or south of the equator
Distance east or west of the prime meridian

units.t: Early Humans and the Agricultural Revolution
learn: Archaeologists study artifacts, such as tools and bones, to learn about the past. Evidence shows modern humans first appeared in Africa roughly 300,000 years ago and spread across the world.
During the Paleolithic era, or Old Stone Age, people were hunter-gatherers. They moved with the seasons, made stone tools, used fire, and created cave paintings.
Around 10,000 BCE, people in several places began farming and herding animals. This change, called the Neolithic or Agricultural Revolution, let people settle in permanent villages.
Farming created food surpluses, so not everyone had to farm. People could become specialized workers, such as potters and builders, which led to trade, towns and eventually cities.
units.try: Imagine you are a hunter-gatherer. List five things you would need to survive one season. Then list how your life would change if your group began farming.
check: What did the Agricultural Revolution allow people to do?
Who studies artifacts to learn about the past?

learn: Mesopotamia means land between the rivers. It lay between the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers in present-day Iraq, part of a region called the Fertile Crescent.
Around 3500 BCE, the Sumerians built some of the first cities, such as Ur and Uruk. They used irrigation canals to water crops. Each city-state had its own ruler and a temple called a ziggurat.

Sumerians invented cuneiform, one of the first writing systems, made by pressing wedge shapes into clay. They also developed the wheel, the plow and a number system based on 60, which is why we have 60 minutes in an hour.

Later, King Hammurabi of Babylon wrote a law code around 1750 BCE with 282 laws. Punishments were harsh and depended on a person’s social class, but it showed that laws could be written down for all to see.
units.try: Make your own cuneiform. Flatten a piece of clay or play dough and press a craft stick or pencil edge into it to write your initials using only wedge shapes.
check: Which two rivers were in Mesopotamia?

learn: Ancient Egypt grew along the Nile River in northeast Africa. Each year the Nile flooded and left rich black soil, which let farmers grow wheat, barley and flax in a desert land.
Egypt was united around 3100 BCE and ruled by pharaohs for nearly 3,000 years. Egyptians believed the pharaoh was a god-king.

Egyptians believed in life after death. They preserved bodies as mummies and built tombs. The Great Pyramid of Giza, built around 2560 BCE, was the tallest human-made structure for thousands of years.
Egyptians wrote in hieroglyphics, using picture symbols, on papyrus made from reeds. The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, had the same text in three scripts and helped scholars decode hieroglyphics.
units.try: Design a cartouche, an oval frame Egyptians used for royal names. Draw an oval and fill it with your own picture symbols that stand for the sounds or meaning of your name.
check: Why was the Nile’s flood important?
It left fertile soil for farming

learn: One of the first civilizations in South Asia grew in the Indus River Valley around 2500 BCE. Cities like Harappa and Mohenjo-daro had grid streets, brick houses and advanced drainage systems.

Later, people speaking Indo-Aryan languages composed sacred texts called the Vedas. Over time, society was divided into groups in a system often called the caste system, which limited people’s jobs and social lives by birth.

Hinduism developed from these traditions and teaches ideas such as dharma (duty), karma (actions have consequences) and reincarnation. Buddhism began with Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, around 500 BCE, and teaches the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path.

The Maurya Empire’s Emperor Ashoka converted to Buddhism and spread messages of nonviolence. The Gupta Empire later saw advances in math, including the concept of zero and the decimal number system we use today.
units.try: Look at the digits 0 to 9 that we use every day. Write a short paragraph explaining how math would be harder without a symbol for zero, an idea developed by mathematicians in ancient India.
check: Which river valley held an early Indian civilization?

learn: Chinese civilization grew along the Huang He (Yellow River) and Yangtze River. The Shang dynasty, around 1600 BCE, left writing on oracle bones, the ancestor of Chinese characters.

Chinese rulers claimed the Mandate of Heaven, the idea that heaven gave a ruler the right to rule. If a ruler was unjust, floods or rebellions were seen as signs the mandate was lost, and a new dynasty could take over.
Confucius taught that society works best when people respect family, elders and proper relationships, and when leaders rule by good example. Daoism taught living in harmony with nature.
The Qin dynasty united China in 221 BCE and began the Great Wall. The Han dynasty invented paper and expanded the Silk Road, trade routes linking China to Central Asia and the Mediterranean.
units.try: Make a timeline of five Chinese inventions: paper, silk, the compass, porcelain and printing. For each, write one way it is still used in your life today.
check: What was the Mandate of Heaven?
The belief that heaven gave rulers the right to rule
What did the Silk Road connect?
China with Central Asia and the Mediterranean

learn: Greece is a mountainous land with many islands, so Greeks lived in separate city-states, each called a polis. Two famous ones were Athens and Sparta.

Athens developed the first known democracy around 500 BCE, where citizens voted directly on laws. Only free adult men born in Athens were citizens; women, enslaved people and foreigners could not vote.
Sparta focused on military strength; boys trained as soldiers from age 7. Athens and Sparta united against Persia but later fought each other in the Peloponnesian War.

Greek thinkers like Socrates, Plato and Aristotle shaped philosophy. Greeks also gave us the Olympic Games, theater, geometry from Euclid, and architecture with columns. Alexander the Great spread Greek culture from Egypt to India.
units.try: Hold a mini Athenian assembly at dinner. Propose a family rule, let each person speak for one minute, and then vote. Discuss: who would have been allowed to vote in ancient Athens?
check: Who could vote in Athenian democracy?
Free adult men who were citizens

learn: Rome began as a small city in Italy. In 509 BCE, Romans set up a republic, where citizens elected leaders. The Senate and two consuls governed, and the Twelve Tables were Rome’s written laws.
Rome grew through conquest and trade until it controlled the whole Mediterranean. After Julius Caesar took power and was killed in 44 BCE, his heir Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BCE.

The Pax Romana was about 200 years of relative peace. Romans built roads, aqueducts that carried water, and concrete structures like the Colosseum. Latin became the root of Spanish, French and Italian.

Christianity began in the Roman province of Judea and spread across the empire. The Western Roman Empire fell in 476 CE due to weak leaders, money troubles and invasions; the Eastern part lasted as the Byzantine Empire.
units.try: Find ten English words with Latin roots, such as aqua (water) in aquarium. Write the Latin root and the meaning next to each word.
check: What kind of government did Rome have before emperors?
A democracy where all voted directly

learn: The Olmec of Mexico, around 1200 BCE, are one of the earliest civilizations in the Americas. They carved giant stone heads and influenced later cultures.
The Maya built city-states in southern Mexico and Central America. They created a writing system, an accurate calendar, and pyramids. Maya mathematicians used a symbol for zero.
The Aztecs founded Tenochtitlan in 1325 on an island in a lake, where Mexico City is today. They farmed on floating gardens called chinampas.
The Inca built an empire along the Andes Mountains in South America, linked by about 40,000 kilometers of roads. They farmed on terraces and kept records with knotted cords called quipu.
units.try: Draw a cross-section of a hillside with Inca terraces. Explain in two sentences how flat steps on a mountain help farmers grow crops and keep soil from washing away.
check: On an island in a lake
On the banks of the Nile
What did the Inca use quipu for?

learn: Geographers divide the world into regions that share features. Physical regions share landforms or climate, like the Sahara Desert. Cultural regions share language, religion or customs, like Latin America.
Population is not spread evenly. More than half of the world’s 8 billion people live in Asia. Most people live near water, fertile land and mild climates.
Culture includes language, religion, food, clothing, art and traditions. Cultures spread through trade, migration and communication, a process called cultural diffusion.
Many ancient ideas still shape the world: writing, law codes, democracy, religions, mathematics and city planning. Studying the past helps us understand why places are the way they are.
units.try: Pick one country on a different continent. Find its capital, main languages, climate and one traditional food. Then name one idea or invention from the ancient world that people there still use.
check: The spread of culture from place to place
Which continent has the most people?

rooms.about: This year you will begin speaking, reading and writing Spanish: greetings, numbers, colors, family, school and food. You will also discover the cultures of the more than 20 countries where Spanish is an official language.

learn: Spanish is spoken by over 500 million people and is an official language in 20 countries plus Puerto Rico. Spanish vowels have one clear sound each: a (ah), e (eh), i (ee), o (oh), u (oo).

Greetings: Hola (hello), Buenos días (good morning), Buenas tardes (good afternoon), Buenas noches (good evening or good night). Goodbyes: Adiós, Hasta luego (see you later), Hasta mañana (see you tomorrow).
To introduce yourself: ¿Cómo te llamas? (What is your name?) Me llamo Ana. (My name is Ana.) Mucho gusto means nice to meet you.
To ask how someone is: ¿Cómo estás? Answers: Bien (well), Muy bien (very well), Más o menos (so-so), Mal (bad). Add y tú? to ask back: and you?
units.try: Practice a conversation out loud with a family member. A: Hola, ¿cómo te llamas? B: Me llamo ___. ¿Y tú? A: Me llamo ___. Mucho gusto. B: Igualmente. ¿Cómo estás? A: Muy bien, gracias.
check: How do you say good morning?

learn: The Spanish alphabet has 27 letters, including ñ (eñe), as in niño (child) and año (year). The letters ch and ll are now treated as pairs of letters, not separate letters.
The letter h is always silent: hola sounds like oh-la. The letter j sounds like a strong English h: jugo (juice). The letters ll usually sound like the y in yes: llama.
A single r between vowels is a quick tap, as in pero (but). The rr and an r at the start of a word are rolled or trilled, as in perro (dog) and rojo (red).
Accent marks show which syllable to stress: teléfono, música. They can also change meaning: sí means yes, and si means if.
units.try: Spell your name out loud using Spanish letter names: a, be, ce, de, e, efe, ge, hache, i, jota, ka, ele, eme, ene, eñe, o, pe, cu, erre, ese, te, u, uve, uve doble, equis, ye, zeta.
check: Which letter is always silent in Spanish?

learn: Numbers 1 to 10: uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez. 11 to 15: once, doce, trece, catorce, quince. 16 to 19 combine words: dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve. 20 is veinte, 30 is treinta.
Days of the week are lowercase in Spanish: lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo. Many calendars in Spanish-speaking countries start with Monday.
Months are also lowercase: enero, febrero, marzo, abril, mayo, junio, julio, agosto, septiembre, octubre, noviembre, diciembre.
To give a date, say the day number first: Hoy es el cinco de mayo (Today is May fifth). For the first of the month, many people say el primero de enero.
units.try: Say today’s date in Spanish: Hoy es (day of the week), el (number) de (month). Then say your birthday: Mi cumpleaños es el ___ de ___.

learn: Colors: rojo (red), azul (blue), amarillo (yellow), verde (green), anaranjado (orange), morado (purple), negro (black), blanco (white), gris (gray), rosado (pink), marrón (brown).
Classroom objects: el lápiz (pencil), el libro (book), el cuaderno (notebook), la mochila (backpack), la silla (chair), la mesa (table), el bolígrafo (pen), la computadora (computer).
Every Spanish noun has a gender. El is used with masculine nouns and la with feminine nouns. Plural: los and las. Many nouns ending in o are masculine and many ending in a are feminine.
In Spanish, colors usually come after the noun and match it: el libro rojo, la mochila roja, los libros rojos. Colors ending in e, like verde, only change for plural: verdes.
units.try: Look around your room and name five objects with their colors in Spanish, for example: la silla negra, el cuaderno azul. Say them aloud, making the color match the noun.
check: How do you say the red backpack?

learn: Family words: la familia, la madre or mamá (mother), el padre or papá (father), el hermano (brother), la hermana (sister), el abuelo (grandfather), la abuela (grandmother), el tío (uncle), la tía (aunt), el primo and la prima (cousins).
To say what someone has: Tengo dos hermanos (I have two brothers or siblings). A masculine plural can include both genders.
To describe people, use ser (to be): Soy alto (I am tall). Ella es simpática (She is nice). Adjectives match the person: alto, alta, altos, altas.
Useful adjectives: alto (tall), bajo (short), simpático (nice), inteligente (smart), divertido (fun), trabajador (hardworking), joven (young), mayor (older).
units.try: Draw your family tree, real or imaginary, and label each person in Spanish. Write one sentence about each: Mi abuela es simpática y divertida.
check: Which correctly describes a girl as tall?

units.t: The Verb Ser and Subject Pronouns
learn: Subject pronouns: yo (I), tú (you, informal), usted (you, formal), él (he), ella (she), nosotros or nosotras (we), ustedes (you all), ellos or ellas (they).

Use tú with friends, family and children. Use usted with adults you respect, like a teacher or a stranger. In Spain, vosotros is used for you all with friends; in Latin America, ustedes is used for everyone.
Ser means to be for identity, origin and traits: yo soy, tú eres, él or ella or usted es, nosotros somos, ellos or ustedes son.
Use ser de to say where someone is from: Soy de Texas. Ella es de México. ¿De dónde eres? means Where are you from?
units.try: Write four sentences with ser: one about you, one about a friend, one about your family (nosotros) and one about two people you admire (ellos). Say where each is from.
check: Which pronoun would you use with a teacher?

learn: School subjects: las matemáticas, las ciencias, el inglés, el español, la historia, el arte, la música, la educación física.
To tell time, use ser: ¿Qué hora es? Es la una (It is 1:00). Son las tres (It is 3:00). Son las cuatro y media (4:30). Son las dos y cuarto (2:15).
To say when something happens, use a: La clase de arte es a las diez (Art class is at ten).
Opinions: Me gusta la música (I like music). No me gusta la historia (I do not like history). Use me gustan with plural: Me gustan las ciencias.
units.try: Write your daily school schedule in Spanish. For each class, write the time and your opinion: Tengo matemáticas a las nueve. Me gustan las matemáticas.
check: How do you say It is 3:30?
How do you say I like science (plural)?

learn: Foods: el pan (bread), el arroz (rice), los frijoles (beans), el pollo (chicken), el pescado (fish), la fruta (fruit), la manzana (apple), el queso (cheese), la ensalada (salad). Drinks: el agua (water), la leche (milk), el jugo (juice).
Meals: el desayuno (breakfast), el almuerzo (lunch), la cena (dinner). In many Spanish-speaking countries lunch is the largest meal, often eaten around 2 p.m.
To order politely: Quisiera un jugo, por favor (I would like a juice, please). To ask the price: ¿Cuánto cuesta? Say gracias (thank you) and de nada (you are welcome).
Foods connect to culture: tortillas and tamales in Mexico, arepas in Venezuela and Colombia, paella in Spain, empanadas in Argentina and many other countries.
units.try: Act out a restaurant scene. One person is the server: ¿Qué quieres comer? The other orders: Quisiera el pollo con arroz y un agua, por favor. Switch roles.
check: How do you politely say I would like?

learn: Verbs in the infinitive form end in -ar, -er or -ir: hablar (to speak), comer (to eat), vivir (to live). To conjugate an -ar verb, remove -ar and add endings.
Hablar: yo hablo, tú hablas, él or ella habla, nosotros hablamos, ellos or ustedes hablan.
Other -ar verbs: estudiar (to study), bailar (to dance), cantar (to sing), caminar (to walk), escuchar (to listen), nadar (to swim), tomar (to take or drink).
Because the ending shows who does the action, Spanish often drops the subject pronoun: Hablo español means I speak Spanish.
units.try: Conjugate bailar for all five forms. Then write three sentences about what you and your family do on weekends, like Mi hermano nada en la piscina.
check: What is the yo form of estudiar?

learn: Spanish-speaking countries are found in Europe (Spain), North America (Mexico), Central America, the Caribbean (Cuba, Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico), South America and Africa (Equatorial Guinea).
Mexico has the most Spanish speakers, over 120 million. The United States has more than 40 million people who speak Spanish at home.
Celebrations include Día de los Muertos in Mexico (November 1 and 2), honoring loved ones who have died with altars and marigolds, and Las Fallas in Valencia, Spain.
Each country has its own accents, words and foods. For example, a bus is el autobús in many places, la guagua in Cuba and Puerto Rico, and el camión in Mexico.
units.try: Choose one Spanish-speaking country. Find its capital, flag colors and one tradition. Make a small poster in Spanish: La capital es ___. La bandera es ___ y ___.
check: Which country has the most Spanish speakers?
Which African country has Spanish as an official language?

rooms.about: This year you will build skills in drawing, painting, printmaking and sculpture using the elements of art and principles of design. You will also study art from around the world and learn to talk about artworks.

learn: The elements of art are the building blocks of every artwork: line, shape, form, color, value, texture and space.
Line is a mark that moves through space; it can be thick, thin, curved or zigzag. Shape is flat and two-dimensional, like a circle. Form is three-dimensional, like a sphere.

Value is how light or dark something is. Texture is how something feels or looks like it would feel. Space is the area around and between objects; positive space is the object and negative space is the area around it.
Artists choose and combine elements on purpose. A drawing with only sharp diagonal lines feels energetic; one with soft curves feels calm.
units.try: Fold a paper into seven boxes. In each box, draw a small example of one element of art and label it. For texture, try making tree bark, fur and brick with only a pencil.
check: How light or dark something is

learn: The principles of design describe how artists arrange elements: balance, contrast, emphasis, movement, pattern, rhythm, proportion and unity.
Balance can be symmetrical, the same on both sides, or asymmetrical, different but equal in visual weight. Radial balance spreads out from a center, like a flower.
Emphasis creates a focal point, the first place your eye goes. Artists use contrast in color, size or detail to make it stand out.
Unity is the feeling that everything belongs together. Repeating colors or shapes helps create unity, while variety keeps the work interesting.
units.try: Make two small collages from magazine scraps or colored paper: one with symmetrical balance and one with asymmetrical balance. Which one feels calmer? Which feels more exciting?
check: The place your eye goes first
What kind of balance spreads from a center?

learn: Observational drawing means drawing what you actually see instead of what you think something looks like. Slow looking is the main skill.

Contour drawing traces the outer and inner edges of an object with one continuous line. Blind contour drawing means looking only at the object, not the paper; it trains your eye and hand to work together.
Gesture drawing uses quick, loose lines to capture movement and pose in 30 seconds to 2 minutes.
Measure proportions by holding your pencil at arm’s length and comparing sizes, such as how many head-lengths tall a person is. Adults are usually about seven to eight heads tall.
units.try: Do a blind contour drawing of your non-drawing hand for 3 minutes. Then do a regular contour drawing for 5 minutes. Compare them and notice what you saw more carefully.
check: Drawing while looking only at the object
Drawing with your eyes closed from memory
About how many heads tall is an adult?

learn: Shading uses value to make flat shapes look three-dimensional. A value scale shows steps from white to black.

When light hits a sphere, you see a highlight (the brightest spot), mid-tones, a core shadow (darkest part on the object), reflected light near the bottom edge, and a cast shadow on the surface below.
Shading techniques include hatching (parallel lines), cross-hatching (crossing lines), stippling (dots) and blending (smooth tones with a soft tool or finger).
Pencils are graded by hardness. H pencils are hard and light; B pencils are soft and dark. A 2B or 4B pencil is good for shading.
units.try: Draw a five-step value scale. Then draw a circle, choose where the light comes from, and shade it into a sphere with a highlight, core shadow and cast shadow.

learn: The primary colors in paint are red, yellow and blue. Mixing two primaries makes secondary colors: orange, green and violet. Mixing a primary and a neighboring secondary makes tertiary colors like red-orange.

The color wheel arranges these 12 colors in a circle. Complementary colors sit opposite each other, like blue and orange; they create strong contrast. Analogous colors sit next to each other and look harmonious.
A tint is a color plus white; a shade is a color plus black; a tone is a color plus gray.
Warm colors (red, orange, yellow) seem to come forward and feel energetic. Cool colors (blue, green, violet) seem to recede and feel calm.
units.try: With paints, colored pencils or markers, make your own 12-part color wheel. Then paint a small landscape using only analogous colors.
check: What is the complement of blue?

learn: Perspective makes a flat picture look deep. Simple tricks: overlap objects, make far objects smaller, place them higher on the page, and use less detail and duller color for distant things.
Linear perspective uses a horizon line at eye level and vanishing points where parallel lines seem to meet. Renaissance artist Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated it in the early 1400s.
In one-point perspective, lines going away from you meet at one vanishing point, like railroad tracks.
In two-point perspective, an object is seen from a corner, and lines run to two vanishing points on the horizon. This is useful for drawing buildings.
units.try: Draw a horizon line and one vanishing point in the middle. Draw a road that narrows toward the point, then add trees and poles that get smaller as they approach it.
check: Where is the horizon line in perspective drawing?
In one-point perspective, lines going away meet at what?

learn: Printmaking makes copies of an image by transferring ink from a prepared surface, called a matrix or plate, to paper. Each copy is called a print.

In relief printing, you carve away areas you do not want to print. The raised areas get ink. Woodcuts and linocuts are relief prints. Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock prints, like Hokusai’s Great Wave, are famous examples.
Remember the image prints in reverse, so letters must be carved backward.
A series of identical prints is called an edition. Artists number them, like 3/20, meaning the third print of twenty.
units.try: Make a foam or cardboard print. Press a dull pencil into a clean foam tray to draw a design, roll or brush on washable paint, press paper on top and peel it off. Try two colors.
check: In relief printing, which areas get ink?
Why must letters be carved backward?

learn: Sculpture is three-dimensional art. Additive sculpture builds up material, like modeling clay. Subtractive sculpture removes material, like carving stone or wood.
Assemblage sculpture joins found objects together. Relief sculpture projects from a flat background, like faces on coins.
Sculptors think about form, mass, balance and how the work looks from all sides. A freestanding sculpture can be viewed in the round.
Clay techniques include the pinch pot, the coil method and the slab method. Pieces are joined by scoring (scratching) and adding slip (watery clay).
units.try: Make a small pinch pot from air-dry clay or play dough. Push your thumb into a ball and pinch the sides while turning. Add a texture to the outside with a fork or a leaf.
check: How do you join two pieces of clay?

learn: People in every culture make art. The cave paintings at Lascaux in France are about 17,000 years old. Aboriginal Australian art includes dot paintings that can tell stories about land and ancestors.
West African masks, often carved from wood, are used in ceremonies and dances. Chinese ink-and-brush painting values few strokes and empty space.
Islamic art often uses geometric patterns, flowing calligraphy and repeating vine designs called arabesques.
Mexican artists like Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera drew on Indigenous traditions; Rivera painted huge murals showing workers and history.
units.try: Design a tile using a repeating geometric pattern inspired by Islamic art. Start with a circle, divide it with a ruler into equal parts, and connect points to make a star.
check: Who painted large murals about Mexican history and workers?

learn: A critique is a careful discussion of an artwork. One common method has four steps: describe, analyze, interpret and judge.
Describe: list what you see without opinions. Analyze: explain how the elements and principles are used. Interpret: say what you think the work means or expresses.
Judge: decide if the work is successful and explain why using evidence. Saying I like it is not enough; explain what works and why.
When giving feedback to classmates, be kind, specific and helpful. A good pattern is to name a strength, ask a question, and offer one suggestion.
units.try: Choose any artwork, from a book, museum or your own home. Write four sentences, one for each critique step. Then share it with a family member and see if they agree.
check: What is the first step of a critique?
The shadows make the apple look round

rooms.about: This year you will read rhythms and melodies in standard notation, learn about instruments and the orchestra, explore music from many cultures and styles, and create and perform your own short pieces.

learn: Music has basic elements: rhythm (patterns of long and short sounds), melody (a series of pitches), harmony (pitches sounding together), timbre (tone color), dynamics (loud and soft), tempo (speed) and form (structure).
Pitch is how high or low a sound is. It depends on frequency, measured in hertz. The A above middle C is usually tuned to 440 hertz.
Timbre is what makes a flute sound different from a trumpet playing the same note.
Listening for elements helps you describe music. Instead of saying a song is cool, you can say it has a fast tempo, loud dynamics and a repeating melody.
units.try: Listen to any song for one minute. Write one word or phrase for each element: rhythm, melody, harmony, timbre, dynamics, tempo and form.
check: The tone color of a sound

learn: The beat is the steady pulse of music. Rhythm is the pattern of sounds placed over the beat.
In 4/4 time, a whole note lasts 4 beats, a half note 2 beats, a quarter note 1 beat, and an eighth note half a beat. A dot after a note adds half its value, so a dotted half note lasts 3 beats.
Rests are silences with the same values: whole rest, half rest, quarter rest and eighth rest.
A time signature has two numbers. The top shows beats per measure; the bottom shows which note gets the beat. In 3/4, there are 3 quarter-note beats per measure, used for waltzes.
units.try: Count and clap this 4/4 pattern: quarter, quarter, half (1, 2, 3-4). Then: eighth, eighth, quarter, quarter rest, quarter (1-and, 2, rest, 4). Make up your own 4-measure pattern.
check: How many beats does a half note get in 4/4?
How many beats are in a measure of 3/4?

learn: Music is written on a staff of five lines and four spaces. A clef at the start tells which pitches the lines stand for.
In treble clef, the lines from bottom to top are E, G, B, D, F (Every Good Bird Does Fly). The spaces spell F, A, C, E.
In bass clef, used for lower instruments, the lines are G, B, D, F, A and the spaces are A, C, E, G.

Musical letter names go A through G and then repeat. Middle C sits on a short extra line, called a ledger line, between the two staves. A sharp (♯) raises a note a half step; a flat (♭) lowers it a half step.
units.try: Draw a treble staff. Write notes on the lines and spaces to spell these words: CAGE, BED, FACE. Then check them with the memory phrases.
check: What are the treble clef spaces from bottom to top?
Raises a note a half step
Lowers a note a half step

learn: A scale is a set of pitches in order. A major scale has the pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half steps. C major uses only the white keys: C D E F G A B C.
Major scales often sound bright; natural minor scales often sound darker. A minor uses the white keys starting on A.
A melody moves by step (to the next note) or by leap (skipping notes). Most memorable melodies use mostly steps with a few leaps.
The pentatonic scale has five notes, such as C D E G A. It appears in folk music from many cultures, including China, West Africa, Scotland and Indigenous American traditions.
units.try: Sing do-re-mi-fa-sol-la-ti-do up and down slowly. Then create a short melody using only the pentatonic notes do, re, mi, sol and la. Sing or hum it three times.
check: How many notes are in a pentatonic scale?
Which scale uses only white keys starting on C?

learn: Orchestra instruments are grouped into four families. Strings: violin, viola, cello, double bass, harp. Woodwinds: flute, clarinet, oboe, bassoon.
Brass: trumpet, French horn, trombone, tuba. Brass players buzz their lips into a mouthpiece. Percussion: timpani, snare drum, cymbals, xylophone; these are struck, shaken or scraped.
Larger instruments usually make lower sounds. The tuba is the lowest brass instrument and the piccolo is the highest woodwind.
A conductor leads the orchestra, showing the beat and tempo with hand patterns or a baton. A symphony orchestra may have about 80 to 100 musicians.
units.try: Make a simple string instrument: stretch rubber bands of different thicknesses around an open box. Pluck each one. Which makes the lowest sound? Why?
check: Which family does the clarinet belong to?
Which instrument plays the lowest pitches?

learn: Form is the plan or structure of a piece. Musicians label sections with letters: A for the first idea, B for a contrasting idea.
Binary form is AB. Ternary form is ABA: an idea, a contrast, and a return. Rondo form brings back A between new sections: ABACA.
Many popular songs use verse-chorus form. Verses tell the story with changing words; the chorus repeats the main message with the same words. A bridge adds contrast near the end.
Theme and variations presents a melody and then changes it in rhythm, harmony, tempo or style.
units.try: Listen to a favorite song and map its form with letters, such as intro, verse, chorus, verse, chorus, bridge, chorus. Count how many times the chorus repeats.
check: Which part of a song usually repeats the same words?

learn: Dynamics are written in Italian. Piano (p) means soft and forte (f) means loud. Mezzo means medium: mezzo piano (mp) and mezzo forte (mf). Pianissimo (pp) is very soft and fortissimo (ff) is very loud.
A crescendo means gradually get louder; a decrescendo or diminuendo means gradually get softer.
Tempo markings: largo (very slow), adagio (slow), andante (walking speed), moderato (medium), allegro (fast), presto (very fast). Tempo can also be marked in beats per minute.
Articulation shows how notes are played: staccato (short, detached), legato (smooth, connected) and accent (emphasized).
units.try: Sing or hum a simple song like Happy Birthday four ways: pianissimo and slow, fortissimo and fast, with a crescendo, and staccato. Notice how each changes the feeling.

learn: Every culture makes music. West African drumming often uses polyrhythm, two or more rhythms played at once, and call and response between a leader and a group.
Indian classical music uses ragas (melodic frameworks) and talas (rhythmic cycles). Instruments include the sitar and tabla drums.
Indonesian gamelan ensembles feature bronze gongs and metallophones playing interlocking patterns. Andean music from Peru and Bolivia uses panpipes called siku and the small guitar called charango.
Mariachi from Mexico features violins, trumpets and guitars like the vihuela and guitarrón. Music often goes with dance, celebration and storytelling.
units.try: Make a call-and-response game. One person claps a 4-beat rhythm (the call), and everyone else answers with a different 4-beat rhythm (the response). Take turns being the leader.
check: Two or more rhythms played at once

learn: Spirituals were religious songs created by enslaved African Americans. They blended African musical traditions with Christian hymns and sometimes carried hidden messages of hope and escape.
The blues developed in the Mississippi Delta in the late 1800s. A 12-bar blues uses three chords in a set pattern, and lyrics often follow an AAB pattern.
Jazz began in New Orleans in the early 1900s. It features improvisation, which is making up music on the spot, and swing rhythms. Louis Armstrong and Duke Ellington were important jazz musicians.
Blues and jazz influenced rock and roll, soul, funk and hip-hop. Country music grew from folk traditions in the South, and Latin music shaped styles like salsa.
units.try: Make up a two-line blues verse in AAB form about something small, like a lost sock. Sing line A twice, then answer it with line B.
check: Making up music on the spot

learn: Composing means creating original music and writing it down. Start small: choose a time signature, a key and a mood. Write a 4-measure rhythm, then add pitches.
Melodies often end on the home note, called the tonic, which makes them sound finished.
Good performers prepare by practicing in short focused sessions, slowing down hard parts, and then speeding up. Warm up your voice or body first.
Stage presence includes good posture, entering and exiting calmly, and bowing to say thank you. Audience etiquette means listening quietly and clapping at the end of a piece.
units.try: Compose an 8-measure melody in 4/4 using C D E F G. End on C. Practice it on a keyboard app, a recorder or by singing with letter names, then perform it for your family.
check: The home note of a key
The first note in any song
Listening quietly and clapping at the end

rooms.about: This year you will learn the parts of fitness, how to plan safe workouts, and skills for team and individual sports. In health, you will study nutrition, sleep, growing up, feelings, friendships and staying safe.

learn: Health-related fitness has five parts: cardiorespiratory endurance (heart and lungs), muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition.
Muscular strength is how much force a muscle can make once. Muscular endurance is how many times it can work without tiring, like doing many push-ups.
Skill-related fitness includes agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed. These help in sports and games.
Experts recommend that kids and teens get at least 60 minutes of physical activity every day, including vigorous activity and muscle and bone strengthening at least 3 days a week.
units.try: Test yourself safely: count how many jumping jacks you can do in 30 seconds, hold a plank as long as you can with good form, and do a sit-and-reach stretch. Write your scores and retest in a month.
check: Which is part of health-related fitness?
How much daily activity is recommended for teens?

units.t: Warming Up, Cooling Down and the FITT Principle
learn: A warm-up raises your heart rate and loosens muscles before exercise. Spend 5 to 10 minutes on light jogging and dynamic stretches, like arm circles and leg swings.
A cool-down lets your heart rate return to normal. Walk slowly, then do static stretches, holding each for 15 to 30 seconds without bouncing.
The FITT principle helps you plan workouts: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long) and Type (what activity).
To improve, change one FITT part slowly, like adding 5 minutes a week. This is called progression. Rest days help muscles repair.
units.try: Plan a one-week activity schedule using FITT. Example: Frequency 4 days, Intensity moderate, Time 30 minutes, Type biking. Include a warm-up and cool-down each day.
check: What does the I in FITT stand for?
When should you do static stretches?

learn: Your heart is a muscle that pumps blood carrying oxygen. Cardio exercise, like running, swimming, dancing and biking, makes your heart stronger.
To find your pulse, put two fingers on the side of your neck or inside your wrist. Count beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4 to get beats per minute.
A typical resting heart rate for kids your age is about 60 to 100 beats per minute. Regular exercise can lower your resting heart rate over time because the heart becomes more efficient.
Use the talk test: during moderate activity you can talk but not sing; during vigorous activity you can say only a few words before needing a breath.
units.try: Measure your resting pulse. Then jog in place for 2 minutes and measure again. Rest for 2 minutes and measure a third time. How quickly does it come back down?
check: How do you get beats per minute from a 15-second count?
During vigorous activity, the talk test shows you can do what?

learn: Most team sports involve offense (trying to score) and defense (trying to stop scoring). Invasion games like soccer and basketball require moving into the other team’s space.
Offensive strategies include spreading out, moving to open space and passing quickly. Defensive strategies include staying between your opponent and the goal and communicating with teammates.
Basic skills include passing, receiving, dribbling and shooting. Practice with both your dominant and non-dominant side.
Good sportsmanship means following rules, respecting officials, encouraging teammates and shaking hands after games, whether you win or lose.
units.try: With a ball and a wall, practice passing 20 times with your right foot or hand and 20 times with your left. Count how many clean catches or traps you make each time.
check: What is a good offensive strategy?

learn: Nutrients your body needs include carbohydrates (main energy source), proteins (build and repair tissues), fats (energy and cell health), vitamins, minerals and water.
A healthy plate is about half fruits and vegetables, a quarter grains (preferably whole grains) and a quarter protein, with a serving of dairy or a calcium-rich food.
Nutrition labels show serving size, calories and nutrients. The percent daily value tells how much one serving gives of a day’s needs; 5% or less is low, 20% or more is high.
Limit added sugars, sodium and saturated fat. Drink water instead of sugary drinks, and eat breakfast to fuel your brain for school.
units.try: Look at the nutrition label on two snack foods at home. Compare serving size, added sugars and fiber. Which is the better everyday choice, and why?
check: What is the body’s main energy source?
On a label, what percent daily value is considered high?

learn: Kids ages 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night, and teens need about 8 to 10 hours. Sleep helps memory, mood, growth and the immune system.
Good sleep habits: a regular bedtime, a cool dark room, and no screens for 30 to 60 minutes before bed.

Puberty is the time when the body changes from a child to an adult, usually starting between ages 8 and 14. Hormones cause growth spurts, more sweat and oil, and emotional changes. Everyone’s timing is different and normal.
Hygiene becomes more important: shower regularly, use deodorant, wash your face, brush teeth twice a day and floss once a day.
units.try: Track your sleep for a week: bedtime, wake time and how rested you felt. Then pick one sleep habit to improve, such as turning off screens earlier.
check: How much sleep do teens need each night?
What causes the body changes of puberty?

learn: Emotions are normal, and all feelings are okay, even if some actions are not. Naming a feeling, like frustrated or nervous, helps you manage it.
Stress is the body’s response to a challenge. A little stress can help you focus, but too much can cause headaches, trouble sleeping and irritability.
Healthy coping strategies include deep breathing, exercise, talking to someone you trust, writing in a journal, getting enough sleep and breaking big tasks into small steps.
If sadness, worry or anger lasts a long time or feels overwhelming, talk to a parent, school counselor, teacher or doctor. Asking for help is a sign of strength.
units.try: Practice box breathing: breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 4, breathe out for 4, hold for 4. Repeat four times. Notice how your body feels afterward.
check: Which is a healthy way to cope with stress?
Who can you go to for help with strong feelings?

learn: Healthy friendships include respect, trust, honesty, kindness and fairness. Good friends support you and accept you for who you are.
Communication styles: passive (not speaking up), aggressive (attacking others) and assertive (stating your needs clearly and respectfully). Assertive is usually the healthiest.
Use I-messages to share feelings without blaming: I feel upset when plans change at the last minute, because I was looking forward to it.

Bullying is repeated, intentional hurtful behavior where there is an imbalance of power. It can be physical, verbal, social or online. If you see it, do not join in, support the target and tell a trusted adult.
units.try: Turn these blaming statements into I-messages: You never listen to me. You always take my stuff. Practice saying them out loud calmly.
check: Which communication style is usually healthiest?
It is repeated and intentional with a power imbalance

learn: Many injuries can be prevented. Wear a helmet when biking, skating or scootering; a helmet can reduce the risk of serious head injury by a large amount.
Water safety: swim with a buddy where a lifeguard is present, and never dive into shallow or unknown water.

Online safety: keep personal information private, use strong passwords, and tell a trusted adult if anything online makes you uncomfortable. Remember that people online may not be who they say they are.
In an emergency, stay calm, make sure the area is safe, and call 911. Know your address so you can tell the dispatcher.
units.try: Check your safety gear at home. Does your helmet fit snugly, with the front about two finger-widths above your eyebrows? Make a list of emergency numbers and your full address.
check: About two finger-widths above the eyebrows
What number do you call in an emergency in the US?

learn: Lifetime activities are ones you can enjoy at any age, such as walking, hiking, swimming, cycling, dancing, yoga and jump rope.
Individual activities let you set personal goals and track progress, like running a mile faster or holding a yoga pose longer.
A SMART goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. Example: I will jump rope for 5 minutes without stopping by the end of the month.
Choosing activities you enjoy makes it more likely you will stay active your whole life.
units.try: Write one SMART fitness goal for the next four weeks. Practice your activity at least three times a week and record your progress on a calendar.
check: What does the T in SMART stand for?

rooms.course: Grade 6 Computer Science: Computers & Coding Basics
rooms.about: This year you will learn how computers work, how they store information in binary, and how to think like a programmer with algorithms, sequences, loops, conditions, variables and events.

learn: A computer is a machine that takes input, processes it, stores it and produces output. This is called the input-process-output model.
Input devices send data in: keyboard, mouse, microphone, camera, touchscreen. Output devices show results: monitor, speakers, printer.

The CPU (central processing unit) is the brain that follows instructions. RAM is short-term memory used while programs run. Storage, like a hard drive or solid-state drive, keeps files even when the power is off.
Hardware is the physical parts you can touch. Software is the programs and instructions. The operating system is software that manages the hardware and runs other programs.
units.try: Make a list of five devices in your home that contain computers, such as a microwave or a thermostat. For each, name one input and one output.

learn: Computers store everything as bits, which are 0s and 1s, like switches that are off or on. Eight bits make a byte.
Binary is base 2. Each place is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. The binary number 1011 equals 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11.
Letters are stored as numbers using codes. In ASCII, capital A is 65, which is 01000001 in binary.

Pictures are made of tiny dots called pixels. Each pixel’s color is stored as numbers for red, green and blue. Larger files need more bytes: a kilobyte is about 1,000 bytes, a megabyte about 1 million, a gigabyte about 1 billion.
units.try: Convert 13 to binary. Place values: 8, 4, 2, 1. 13 = 8 + 4 + 1, so put 1 under 8, 1 under 4, 0 under 2, 1 under 1: 1101. Now convert 6 and 10 yourself.
check: How many bits are in a byte?

learn: An algorithm is a step-by-step set of instructions to solve a problem or complete a task. A recipe is an everyday algorithm.
Computers follow instructions exactly and in order. This order is called sequence. If steps are out of order or unclear, the result will be wrong.
Good algorithms are precise, have a clear start and end, and handle each step without guessing.
Pseudocode is writing an algorithm in plain, code-like language before programming. For example: start, get two numbers, add them, show the sum, end.
units.try: Write an algorithm for making a peanut-free sandwich so precise that a robot could follow it. Have someone follow your steps exactly as written. Did anything go wrong? Fix it.
check: Why does order matter in sequence?
Computers follow steps exactly in order

learn: A loop repeats a set of instructions. Instead of writing move forward ten times, you write repeat 10 times: move forward.
A count-controlled loop repeats a set number of times. A condition-controlled loop repeats while something is true, like repeat until you reach the wall.
In Python, a count loop looks like: for i in range(5): followed by an indented line such as print(i). This prints 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
Loops make programs shorter, easier to read and easier to change. Be careful of infinite loops that never stop because the condition never becomes false.
units.try: Write pseudocode for drawing a square with a turtle robot using a loop: repeat 4 times: move forward 100, turn right 90. Then change it to draw a triangle. What turn angle do you need? (120)
check: How many times does for i in range(3) run?

learn: A conditional lets a program make a decision. It checks whether a condition is true or false and chooses what to do.
If-then: if it is raining, then take an umbrella. If-then-else: if the score is over 90, show great job; else show keep practicing.
In Python: if age >= 13: print("teen") else: print("kid"). The colon and indentation show which lines belong to each branch.
Conditions use comparison operators: == (equal to), != (not equal), < (less than), > (greater than), <= and >=. Combine conditions with and, or, not.
units.try: Write pseudocode for a thermostat: if temperature < 68, turn heat on; else if temperature > 76, turn cooling on; else do nothing. Test it with 60, 70 and 80.
check: What runs in the else part?
The code when the condition is false
The code when it is true

learn: A variable is a named container that stores a value a program can use and change. Examples: score = 0, name = "Ava".
The equals sign in programming means assign, not equal. score = score + 1 means take the old score, add 1, and store the new value.
Common data types: integers (whole numbers like 7), floats (decimals like 3.5), strings (text in quotes like "hello") and booleans (True or False).
Choose clear variable names like lives_left instead of x. Variables let games keep track of scores, time and players.
units.try: Trace this code on paper: points = 5, then points = points + 3, then points = points * 2. What is points at the end? (16) Now write your own three-line trace.
check: Checks if score equals score plus 1

learn: An event is something that happens that a program can respond to, like a click, key press, or timer finishing.
Event handlers are pieces of code that run when an event happens: when the green flag is clicked, start the game; when the space key is pressed, jump.
Interactive programs wait for events instead of running straight through. Most apps and games are event-driven.
Block-based languages let you snap together event, loop and conditional blocks. They use the same ideas as text languages, just in a visual form.
units.try: Design a simple game on paper. List three events (for example, arrow key pressed, character touches a coin, timer ends) and what the program does for each.
check: What is an event in programming?
Something that happens that the program responds to
A type of loop that never stops
Which is an example of an event?

learn: A bug is an error in a program. Debugging is finding and fixing bugs. Every programmer writes bugs, so debugging is a normal skill.
Syntax errors break the language rules, like a missing parenthesis. Logic errors run but give the wrong result, like using + instead of −.
Debugging strategies: read error messages, test small parts one at a time, add print statements to see values, and explain your code out loud line by line.
Test with different inputs, including edge cases like 0, negative numbers or empty text, to make sure your program works everywhere.
units.try: Find the bug: this pseudocode should print 1 to 5: count = 1, repeat while count < 5: print count, count = count + 1. (It stops at 4; the condition should be count <= 5.)
check: Code that runs but gives a wrong result
Code with a spelling mistake in a keyword
A computer that will not turn on
Which is a good debugging strategy?
Test small parts one at a time
Delete everything and start over immediately

learn: Decomposition means breaking a big problem into smaller, manageable parts. A game can be split into the player, the enemies, the score and the levels.
A function is a named block of code that does one job and can be reused. In Python: def greet(name): followed by an indented print("Hello " + name).
You call a function by its name: greet("Sam") prints Hello Sam. Values passed in, like "Sam", are called arguments.
Abstraction means hiding details you do not need. You can use a function called draw_star() without thinking about every line inside it.
units.try: Decompose the task of planning a birthday party into at least five smaller tasks. Then pick one and break it into steps, like a function with its own instructions.
check: Breaking a problem into smaller parts
To reuse code that does one job

learn: Computers have changed how we learn, work, communicate and shop. They help doctors, scientists, farmers and artists.
Digital citizenship means using technology responsibly: be kind online, respect others’ privacy, and think before you post because posts can be permanent.
Intellectual property means people own the things they create. Give credit when you use someone else’s work, and use images and music that you have permission to use.

Technology can also cause problems, like screen overuse or unequal access. Designers should think about accessibility so people with disabilities can use their programs, for example with captions and screen readers.
units.try: Make a list of your screen time for one day. Sort it into creating, learning, connecting and just watching. Set one goal for a healthy balance.
check: Being a citizen of a computer
Why should you give credit for others’ work?
